original_context: Real analysis: Euclidean distance between two real numbers a,b defined as d(a,b)=|a−b|, as an application of real absolute value, not its definition.
definition: The usual Euclidean metric on the real line ℝ is d:ℝ×ℝ→[0,∞), defined by d(a,b)=|a−b| for every a,b∈ℝ.
reasoning: The existing screened real-absolute-value meaning includes the consequent expression |a−b| for usual real-line distance. This proposal records that already implied construction as a named metric on ℝ, not a new absolute-value operation or an unrelated metric. It is a useful contextual specialization rather than a strictly new independent primitive.

sources.section: Distance, Euclidean space ℝ^n formula (3), restricted to n=1
sources.relevance: Directly checked Euclidean metric formula sqrt(sum_i|x_i-y_i|²); specializing n=1 gives |a−b|, with this specialization explicitly distinguished from verbatim source text.

related_screened_meanings.relation: Contains the same usual-distance identity as an application of absolute value
General metric-space axioms; does not by itself fix the metric on ℝ

comparison.rationale: Reviewed 595 screened and 16 provisional independent meanings; the real absolute-value meaning explicitly gives |a−b| as distance, so this metric is a labeled specialization rather than a genuinely different notion. No provisional record overrides that metric on ℝ. The earlier reviewed first-generation stage records (4 identities) were also compared for overlap; no identical full meaning is being staged twice.

mathematical_assumptions: The ordinary real absolute value is available.
The codomain is [0,∞) with standard order.
The metric is on ℝ, not on an arbitrary ordered field without additional structure.
